I'm currently testing the Dell 32-inch UltraSharp U3226Q, and so far the review is very positive. When HDR is enabled in macOS, this OLED panel delivers outstanding picture quality. I'll be releasing a full hands-on video of the UltraSharp on our YouTube channel.

At the same time, I'd like to mention an important improvement Apple has made to HDR support in macOS 27. On macOS 26 Tahoe, there was a drawback when using a third-party HDR-capable display—HDR couldn't be enabled at the commonly used 2560 x 1440 scaled resolution. Thankfully, the latest macOS version has fixed this issue.

The Problem

If you're using a third-party HDR10-capable display with macOS Tahoe, you'll see a "High Dynamic Range" toggle under Settings → Displays. When you turn that toggle on, you can view HDR content. You can see an example in the screenshot below.

But notice in that same screenshot, I'm running this 4K UHD display at a resolution of 1920 x 1080, which is exactly a 2x pixel upscale of the native 3840 x 2160 resolution.

Most users probably don't want to use 1920 x 1080, because on a 4K display it makes content look far too large. The Dell UltraSharp U3226Q is a 32-inch display, and running it at 1920 x 1080 would drastically reduce your usable screen space.

Fixing this on macOS is simple: just pick a scaled resolution, such as the very common 2560 x 1440 (which is the default setting for Apple's 5K Studio Display). The problem is, when you select a scaled resolution in macOS Tahoe, HDR gets disabled. Note the screenshot below:

You'll see that the "High Dynamic Range" toggle is no longer present—macOS automatically switches back to "Standard Dynamic Range." In other words, when using an HDR display on macOS Tahoe, you have to choose between HDR and your preferred scaled resolution.

Fortunately, this issue has been fixed in macOS 27 Golden Gate. In the screenshot below, you can see that a scaled resolution and HDR can be enabled at the same time. This is a native system option, with no third-party software involved.

So if you're using a third-party HDR display, I think this feature alone is worth upgrading from macOS Tahoe to macOS Golden Gate. Of course, I tested this on my M4 MacBook Pro. I tried the same setting on my M1 Max MacBook Pro, but even running macOS 27, I couldn't select both options simultaneously—so it looks like there are still some hardware limitations.

macOS Golden Gate includes a whole host of new features, which I've mentioned in my Siri AI overview, my top macOS features video, and my full review of macOS 27. One feature related to HDR displays is that macOS 27 provides more comprehensive native HDR support across the entire system.

Compared to macOS Tahoe, you'll see brighter highlights, brighter cursors, and overall higher contrast. Whether you're an Apple Studio Display XDR user, a Pro Display XDR user, or a third-party OLED display user, you'll get a truly outstanding visual experience.

What do you think? Do you use a third-party external display with your Mac? If so, would you consider using an HDR-capable display?
